output.summary: The 2024 revision of the McDonald criteria (Montalban et al., Lancet Neurol 2025) adds the optic nerve as a fifth region, accepts the kFLC index as an alternative to oligoclonal bands, and allows the central vein sign and paramagnetic rim lesions as supporting markers. Lesions in four or five regions establish dissemination in space without a separate test of dissemination in time; with two or three regions, dissemination in time, positive CSF or the central vein sign is needed. In people over 50 or with vascular risk factors, additional supporting evidence is recommended.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not diagnose MS based on non-specific white-matter lesions alone without meeting the 2024 revised McDonald criteria and excluding mimics

Do not attribute the right hand and foot sensory symptoms to carpal tunnel syndrome or an ulnar neuropathy: an ulnar-side hand and lateral foot pain-sensation loss with a contralateral cord lesion is central
Do not use chronic oral corticosteroids as a maintenance treatment for MS — they are ineffective long-term and carry significant harm
Do not administer live-attenuated vaccines after initiation of B-cell depleting therapy (ocrelizumab, ofatumumab) or S1P modulators (fingolimod, ozanimod)
Do not omit spinal-cord MRI in a patient with myelopathic signs even if the brain MRI alone meets DIS criteria — cord lesions change relapse counting and management
required_recommendations: State relapsing-remitting MS by the 2024 McDonald criteria: DIS in three regions (periventricular, infratentorial, spinal cord), completed by DIT from the enhancing left pontine lesion with non-enhancing lesions; the subcortical temporal lesion does not count as a region

Offer methylprednisolone oral 500 mg daily for 5 days (or IV 1 g daily for 3-5 days) for the disabling diplopia, with blood pressure and glucose monitoring (hypertension, obesity, glucose 102 mg/dL); occlude one eye or fit a temporary prism for the diplopia meanwhile
Offer disease-modifying therapy after diagnosis, choosing efficacy by disease activity (two attacks in 3 months, an enhancing pontine lesion)
Before an anti-CD20 or S1P modulator, check HBsAg, anti-HBc, HCV antibody and VZV IgG (HIV already negative) and give any live vaccine at least 4-6 weeks before starting
Treat the vascular comorbidity (hypertension, obesity, raised glucose), which is associated with faster disability accrual in MS

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Daniel Kovacs is a 29-year-old right-handed man with a history of hypertension and obesity who presents to the emergency department with a 1-day history of binocular horizontal diplopia that is most prominent when looking to the left. He first noticed the double vision yesterday morning when he turned to look at his computer monitor and saw two overlapping images side by side. The diplopia resolves when he covers either eye. He describes it as horizontal separation of the two images that becomes worse with leftward gaze and improves somewhat when looking to the right. He has not experienced any eye pain, vision loss, or change in visual acuity. He denies any prior episodes of double vision. On further history, he reports that approximately one to two weeks ago he developed tingling and numbness in his right hand and forearm, predominantly affecting the fourth and fifth fingers and the ulnar aspect of the forearm. He initially attributed this to prolonged keyboard use at work and tried adjusting his workstation ergonomics without improvement. He also notes that around the same time he developed an unusual tingling sensation in the fifth toe of his right foot, which he found odd but did not seek medical attention for. He recalls that roughly three months ago he experienced a similar but more pronounced episode of numbness and paresthesia in the right hand and forearm that lasted approximately two weeks before gradually improving on its own. His primary care physician at that time suspected carpal tunnel syndrome and recommended a wrist splint and anti-inflammatory medication. He has not noticed any significant weakness, difficulty walking, changes in bladder or bowel function, facial weakness, speech changes, swallowing difficulty, or vertigo. He denies any recent infections, fevers, weight loss, skin rashes, joint pain, dry eyes, or dry mouth. He reports mild fatigue over the past several weeks that he attributes to poor sleep habits and work stress. He has no history of seizures or head trauma.

Binocular diplopia resolves with monocular occlusion of either eye. CN VII: No facial asymmetry. CN VIII-XII: Intact.
